sections.title: Two Fundamentally Different Approaches to Code Reuse
sections.content:
**Inheritance** and **composition** are two ways to reuse code and build relationships between classes, but they work in fundamentally different ways. Inheritance establishes an **is-a relationship** at compile time — when you write class Dog extends Animal, you're saying Dog is a specialized kind of Animal that inherits all its behavior and state.

The hierarchy is permanent and fixed. **Composition** establishes a **has-a relationship** at runtime — when Car contains an Engine field, you're saying Car uses an Engine to do its work, but Car can swap that Engine for a different one or work with any object that satisfies the Engine contract. Think of inheritance like being born into a family (you can't change your parents), while composition is like hiring contractors (you can switch who does the work). Composition delegates work to collaborators through their interfaces, creating **loose coupling** because the containing class only knows about the interface contract, not the internal implementation details of the objects it uses.

sections.title: When to Choose Each Approach
sections.content: **Use inheritance** when there's a true taxonomic is-a relationship and you need polymorphism to treat different subclasses uniformly through the parent type, like a payment processing system where CreditCardPayment and PayPalPayment both extend Payment and can be handled by the same processing logic. The subclass should genuinely be a specialized version of the parent in a real-world sense. **Use composition** when you want to reuse behavior but the relationship is about capability rather than identity, like a Car that has an Engine, GPS, and Stereo — the car isn't a kind of engine, it uses an engine. Composition is the default choice when you need runtime flexibility, want to combine multiple behaviors, or need to test classes in isolation. If you're inheriting just to get some utility methods, that's a code smell pointing toward composition.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Inheriting for Code Reuse Alone**: Freshers often extend a class just because it has some useful methods, creating nonsensical is-a relationships like Employee extends Person extends Database just to get database access methods — this creates tight coupling and violates the Liskov Substitution Principle.
- **Not Recognizing Multiple Inheritance Needs**: Java doesn't allow multiple inheritance of classes, so when freshers try to make a class inherit from two parents to get both sets of behavior, they hit a wall — composition solves this by letting a class contain multiple collaborators.
- **Forgetting About Testing**: Freshers don't realize that inheritance makes testing harder because you can't mock the parent class behavior, while composition lets you inject test doubles for every collaborator, enabling true unit testing.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Is-a vs Has-a**: Inheritance models is-a relationships with fixed compile-time hierarchies, composition models has-a relationships with flexible runtime delegation
**Coupling**: Inheritance creates tight coupling because subclasses depend on parent implementation details, composition creates loose coupling through interface contracts
**Gang of Four Principle**: Favor composition over inheritance is a foundational design principle because composition gives more flexibility and maintainability
**Runtime Flexibility**: Composition allows swapping collaborators at runtime through dependency injection, inheritance locks you into compile-time decisions
**Testing**: Composition enables true unit testing by letting you inject mocks, inheritance forces you to test with the real parent class
**Multiple Behaviors**: Composition naturally handles multiple behaviors by containing multiple collaborators, inheritance hits Java's single inheritance limitation
**Encapsulation**: Composition preserves encapsulation by hiding collaborator internals behind interfaces, inheritance exposes parent internals to subclasses

sections.title: Code Example
How to Answer
sections.content: So the core difference is about the relationship type and when it's decided. Inheritance is an is-a relationship that's fixed at compile time — when you write Dog extends Animal, you're saying Dog is a specialized kind of Animal, and it inherits all the parent's methods and fields. That hierarchy can't change. Composition is a has-a relationship that's flexible at runtime — Car has an Engine as a field, and you can swap that Engine for a different one or inject any object that implements the Engine interface. The big practical difference is coupling. With inheritance, the subclass is tightly coupled to the parent's implementation details, not just its public API. If the parent changes internally, it can break subclasses even if the public interface stays the same. That's the fragile base class problem. With composition, you're only coupled to an interface contract, so as long as the interface doesn't change, you can swap implementations freely. That's why the Gang of Four said favor composition over inheritance — it gives you loose coupling, runtime flexibility, and much easier testing because you can inject mocks. You'd use inheritance when there's a true is-a relationship in the real world and you need polymorphism to treat different subclasses uniformly. You'd use composition when you want to combine behaviors, need runtime flexibility, or just want to reuse some functionality without creating a deep inheritance hierarchy. In modern Java with Spring, composition is the default through dependency injection — your services contain repositories and other services as fields, not through inheritance.

direct_answer: Composition is preferred because it creates loose coupling, allows runtime flexibility, and makes testing easier. sections.title: Why Modern Design Favors Composition
sections.content:
The preference for composition over inheritance isn't just theoretical — it solves real problems that plague inheritance-heavy codebases.

The core issue is that **inheritance creates tight coupling** between parent and child classes. A subclass doesn't just depend on the parent's public API, it depends on the entire implementation, including protected methods, internal state, and even the order methods are called. This means **refactoring the parent can break subclasses in unexpected ways**, even when the public contract stays the same. That's the **fragile base class problem**. Composition solves this by making dependencies explicit through **interface contracts**. A class that contains a PaymentProcessor field only depends on the PaymentProcessor interface methods, not on how any particular implementation works internally. This creates **loose coupling** because you can swap in a different PaymentProcessor implementation at runtime, and the containing class doesn't care.

Think of it like using a power outlet — you don't care what's behind the wall generating electricity, you just care about the standard interface. Composition also makes **testing dramatically easier** because you can inject test doubles for every dependency, enabling true unit testing where each class is tested in isolation.

sections.content:

blue|No Fragile Base|~parent change|won't silently break children
emerald|Avoids Deep Trees|~flat design|easier to reason about
violet|Rule|~favor composition|inherit only on a true, stable IS-A

sections.title: Composition Enabling Runtime Flexibility and Testing
Scenarios Where Composition Excels
sections.content:
**When combining multiple behaviors**: If a class needs functionality from multiple sources, composition lets you contain multiple collaborators as fields, while inheritance hits Java's single inheritance wall. A ReportGenerator might need a DataSource, Formatter, and EmailService — you can't inherit from all three, but you can contain all three. **When you need different implementations at runtime**: In a Spring Boot app, you might want to use PostgresUserRepository in production but InMemoryUserRepository in tests, or switch from EmailNotificationService to SmsNotificationService based on user preferences — composition with dependency injection makes this trivial.

**When testing in isolation**: With composition, you inject mocks for all dependencies in your unit tests, so you're only testing the class itself. With inheritance, you're forced to test with the real parent class behavior, making tests slower and more brittle.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Not Understanding Fragile Base Class**: Freshers think as long as they don't change the parent's public methods, subclasses are safe — but changing a protected method or the order of internal calls can break overrides in subclasses.
- **Thinking Inheritance Saves More Code**: Freshers see inheritance as less typing because you get parent methods for free, not realizing that the tight coupling cost far outweighs the small code reuse benefit — composition with small interface contracts is more verbose upfront but much easier to maintain.
- **Ignoring the Testing Story**: Freshers don't think about testing when choosing inheritance, then struggle to write unit tests because they can't mock parent class behavior — with composition, every dependency is mockable through its interface.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Loose Coupling**: Composition couples to interface contracts, inheritance couples to implementation details of the parent class
**Fragile Base Class Problem**: Inheritance makes systems brittle because parent changes can break subclasses even when the public API is unchanged
**Encapsulation Violation**: Inheritance exposes parent internals (protected methods, state) to subclasses, breaking encapsulation guarantees
**Runtime Flexibility**: Composition allows injecting different implementations at runtime through dependency injection, inheritance locks decisions at compile time
**Testability**: Composition enables unit testing by letting you inject mocks, inheritance forces integration testing with real parent behavior
**Single Responsibility**: Composition makes dependencies explicit as constructor parameters, inheritance hides dependencies in the parent class
**Multiple Behaviors**: Composition naturally handles multiple collaborators, inheritance hits Java's single inheritance limitation

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The main reason composition is preferred is it creates loose coupling, which makes code easier to maintain and test. With inheritance, a subclass is tightly coupled to the parent's implementation, not just its public API. That means if you refactor something inside the parent class, even a protected method or the order things happen, you can break subclasses that override behavior. That's called the fragile base class problem, and it makes large inheritance hierarchies really brittle over time. Composition solves this because your class only depends on the interface contract of its collaborators. As long as the interface doesn't change, you can swap in completely different implementations at runtime. In a Spring Boot app, that's exactly what dependency injection does — you declare dependencies as constructor parameters with interface types, and Spring wires in the right implementation at startup. That also makes testing way easier. With composition, you can inject mocks for every dependency in your unit tests, so you're only testing the class itself. With inheritance, you're stuck testing with the real parent class behavior, which is slower and more brittle. Another big advantage is composition handles multiple behaviors naturally. If your class needs functionality from three different sources, you just add three fields. With inheritance, you hit the wall that Java only allows single inheritance. So composition gives you flexibility, testability, and cleaner design. You'd still use inheritance when there's a real is-a relationship and you need polymorphism, but composition is the default choice for code reuse.

Because subclasses depend on the parent's internal implementation details, not just its public interface, any refactor to the parent can have unexpected ripple effects on inherited or overridden behavior in subclasses.

sections.title: Why Parent Class Changes Break Subclasses Unexpectedly
sections.content:
The **fragile base class problem** is a fundamental flaw in inheritance-based design where changes to a parent class can break subclasses in unpredictable ways, even when those changes seem safe and don't modify the public API. The root cause is that subclasses don't just depend on the parent's public interface — they depend on the **entire implementation**, including protected methods, the order methods are called, internal state management, and even assumptions about which methods call which other methods. When a maintainer refactors the parent class, they might change a protected method's signature, add a new step to an internal process, or call methods in a different order. These changes can violate assumptions that subclasses make in their overridden methods, causing bugs that are hard to trace because the parent's public contract stayed the same. It's called fragile base class because the **base (parent) class becomes a fragile foundation** that can't be safely evolved without checking every subclass. This violates the **Open-Closed Principle** — classes should be open for extension but closed for modification — because you can't modify the base without potentially breaking extensions.

The problem gets worse as inheritance hierarchies deepen and more subclasses accumulate.

sections.content:
amber|Fragile Base Class|~the problem|a parent change breaks subclasses|even without editing them
blue|Cause|~hidden coupling|subclass relies on parent internals|self-calls and overrides

violet|The Fix|~composition|delegate to a field, don't inherit

sections.title: How a Safe Parent Refactor Breaks a Subclass
Recognizing and Avoiding the Problem
sections.content:
**Recognize the problem** when you have an inheritance hierarchy and find yourself hesitant to refactor the parent class because you're not sure what subclasses might break, or when you make a seemingly safe parent change and suddenly get bug reports from code that uses subclasses. It's a sign your design has accumulated **implementation coupling**. **Avoid it** by preferring composition over inheritance for code reuse — delegate to collaborators through interface contracts instead of extending parent classes. When you must use inheritance, make the parent class either **completely abstract** with no implementation (just interface-like contracts) or **final** with no intention of subclassing.

Use the **template method pattern** carefully, documenting exactly which methods subclasses can override and which internal methods they must not depend on. Mark methods as final when you don't want subclasses overriding them.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking Public API is the Only Contract**: Freshers believe as long as they don't change public method signatures in the parent, subclasses are safe — but subclasses actually depend on protected methods, internal call order, and implementation details that aren't part of the public API.
- **Not Documenting Override Assumptions**: When writing a parent class, freshers don't document which methods are safe to override and what assumptions subclasses can make, so future maintainers don't know what's safe to change.
- **Using Protected Fields Freely**: Freshers expose fields as protected to let subclasses access them directly, creating tight coupling to the parent's internal state representation — subclasses break when the parent changes from ArrayList to LinkedList or adds validation logic.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Implementation Coupling**: Subclasses depend on parent implementation details, not just the public API, making the parent hard to refactor safely
**Protected Members**: Changes to protected methods or fields can break subclasses even when public methods stay unchanged
**Call Order Dependency**: Subclasses often assume parents call methods in a specific order, so reordering internal calls breaks overrides
**Violates Open-Closed**: The base class can't be closed for modification because changing it risks breaking all subclasses
**Inheritance vs Composition**: Composition avoids this by depending only on interface contracts, not implementation details
**Self-Use Problem**: When a parent method calls another method that subclasses override, refactoring the parent can change which method gets called
**Testing Difficulty**: You can't easily test if a parent change breaks subclasses without running all subclass tests, making refactoring risky

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The fragile base class problem is when you make a change to a parent class that seems totally safe, but it breaks one or more subclasses in unexpected ways. The reason it happens is that subclasses don't just depend on the parent's public methods — they depend on the entire implementation, including protected methods, the order things happen internally, and assumptions about how methods interact. So you might refactor the parent to extract a helper method or change the order of some internal steps, and suddenly subclasses that override certain methods start failing. A classic example is when a parent has an add method that directly modifies a list, and a subclass overrides add to track how many items were added. If the parent gets refactored so add now calls an internal addInternal helper method, and the subclass didn't override that helper, the counting logic breaks even though the parent's public API didn't change at all. It's called fragile base class because the base class becomes this fragile foundation that you can't safely modify without potentially breaking every subclass. This is a major reason why composition is preferred — when you use composition with interfaces, you only depend on the interface contract, not on any implementation details. So you can change the implementation completely without affecting the classes that use it. To avoid the fragile base class problem, favor composition over inheritance, and when you must use inheritance, make parent classes either fully abstract with no implementation, or final so they can't be subclassed. The key insight is that inheritance violates encapsulation by exposing implementation details to subclasses.

question: When is inheritance the right choice over composition?
title: When to use inheritance — valid use cases
direct_answer: Inheritance is the right choice when there's a true is-a relationship where the subclass genuinely is a specialized version of the parent, and you need polymorphism to treat different subclasses uniformly. It's appropriate when the subclass will use most of the parent's behavior and only differs in specific details. The litmus test is whether the subclass is a kind of the parent in a real-world sense, not just borrowing some behavior.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can show balance and nuance, defending inheritance when it's genuinely appropriate rather than dogmatically rejecting it after learning composition is preferred.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying composition is always better without recognizing legitimate use cases for inheritance, which makes you sound inexperienced and dogmatic rather than thoughtful.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Distinguish between taxonomic is-a relationships where inheritance is natural versus behavioral is-a relationships where composition is often better, showing you think critically about design trade-offs.

sections.title: Legitimate Use Cases for Inheritance
sections.content:
While composition is the default choice for code reuse, inheritance has legitimate uses when applied correctly.

The key is recognizing when you have a **true is-a relationship** in the real-world domain, not just a convenience for sharing code. Inheritance is appropriate when you need **polymorphism** to treat different types uniformly through a common interface, and when the subclasses genuinely are specialized versions of the parent that inherit most of its behavior. For example, in a payment system, CreditCardPayment, PayPalPayment, and BankTransferPayment all extend Payment because they truly are kinds of payments, they share common workflow (validate, authorize, capture, record), and you want to write code that processes any Payment without knowing the specific type. The **Liskov Substitution Principle** is the test — you should be able to use a subclass anywhere the parent type is expected without breaking correctness. Inheritance also makes sense for **framework extension points** where the framework provides abstract base classes you're meant to extend, like extending HttpServlet or AbstractController in Spring MVC. The framework uses polymorphism to call your overridden methods at the right lifecycle points.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|True IS-A|~permanent|child is a kind of parent everywhere
blue|Honors LSP|~substitutable|works wherever the base is expected
emerald|Shared Contract|~framework hooks|extend AbstractList, HttpServlet
violet|Avoid When|~reuse only|or the relationship may change → compose

sections.title: Step 1: Verify True Taxonomic Is-A Relationship
sections.content: Ask yourself: in the real-world domain, is the subclass genuinely a kind of the parent? Not just shares some behavior, but actually is a specialized version. **Dog is an Animal** works because in nature, a dog truly is a type of animal — it's a taxonomic relationship. **Employee extends DatabaseConnection** fails this test because an employee is not a kind of database connection, you just want database methods available. A good heuristic is whether you'd use the parent type in a sentence describing the subclass: you'd say a dog is an animal (natural), but you wouldn't say an employee is a database connection (nonsense). Another test is whether the subclass can correctly implement the **Liskov Substitution Principle** — can you use the subclass everywhere the parent is expected without surprising behavior or violations of the parent's contract? If not, you don't have a true is-a relationship.

sections.title: Step 2: Check If You Need Polymorphism
sections.content: Inheritance makes sense when you need to write code that works with the parent type but handles different subclasses at runtime through polymorphism. For example, a PaymentProcessor that takes a Payment parameter can process CreditCardPayment, PayPalPayment, or BankTransferPayment without knowing which one it received — the processor just calls payment.authorize() and the right implementation runs. If you don't need this polymorphic behavior — if every place in your code knows exactly which concrete type it's working with — inheritance is overkill and composition is cleaner. Also consider whether the inheritance hierarchy is shallow (1-2 levels deep). Deep hierarchies (3+ levels) are almost always a mistake because they accumulate fragile base class problems. A shallow hierarchy for clear polymorphism is fine, but deep trees of inheritance are a code smell.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Inheriting for Utility Methods**: Freshers extend a class just to get access to some useful methods without any real is-a relationship, like Employee extends StringUtils to get string formatting methods — this creates nonsensical hierarchies and tight coupling.
- **Dogmatic Composition**: After learning composition is preferred, freshers reject all inheritance and try to use composition even for clear polymorphic scenarios, making the code more complex with unnecessary delegation layers when simple inheritance would be cleaner.
- **Confusing Behavioral Is-A with Taxonomic Is-A**: Freshers see Stack extends Vector in old Java code and think it's good because a stack can do push and pop, but the is-a relationship is wrong because a stack shouldn't expose vector's random access methods — it's behavioral similarity, not taxonomic relationship.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **True Is-A Relationship**: Inheritance is right when the subclass is genuinely a kind of the parent in the real-world domain, not just shares some behavior
**Polymorphism Need**: Use inheritance when you need to treat different subclasses uniformly through the parent type in your code
**Liskov Substitution Principle**: The subclass must be usable anywhere the parent is expected without breaking correctness or surprising behavior
**Shallow Hierarchy**: Inheritance works best in shallow hierarchies (1-2 levels), deep trees accumulate fragile base class problems
**Framework Extension Points**: Inheritance is appropriate when extending framework-provided abstract classes designed for subclassing
**Most Behavior Inherited**: The subclass should use most of the parent's behavior, only adding or specializing specific aspects
**Balance Not Dogma**: Neither favor composition over inheritance nor prefer inheritance is absolute — choose based on the specific design problem

sections.title: Code Example
How to Answer
sections.content: So inheritance is the right choice when you have a true is-a relationship in the real-world domain and you need polymorphism. The key test is whether the subclass genuinely is a kind of the parent, not just shares some behavior. Like if you're building a payment system and you have CreditCardPayment, PayPalPayment, and BankTransferPayment, those really are kinds of payments. They share the same workflow — validate, authorize, capture, record — and you want to write a PaymentProcessor that can handle any Payment without knowing the specific type. That's polymorphism in action. The Liskov Substitution Principle is the formal test — you should be able to use a subclass anywhere the parent type is expected without breaking anything. Another scenario where inheritance makes sense is when you're extending a framework that's designed for it. Like when you extend HttpServlet in Jakarta EE or AbstractController in Spring MVC, you're meant to override specific methods, and the framework uses polymorphism to call your implementation at the right time. You're plugging into an extension point the framework provides. What you don't want is deep inheritance hierarchies or inheriting just to get utility methods. If you're going more than two levels deep, that's usually a design smell. And if you're extending a class just because it has some useful methods, but there's no real is-a relationship, that's a misuse of inheritance — use composition instead. The balance here is that composition should be your default for code reuse, but inheritance is the right tool when you have genuine polymorphism needs and a real taxonomic relationship.

speakable_v2.hook: The Decorator pattern is the textbook example of composition over inheritance, and Java IO uses it everywhere.

beats.content: Instead of creating MilkCoffee, SugarCoffee, and MilkSugarCoffee as separate subclasses, the Decorator pattern creates a MilkDecorator that wraps any Coffee object. It implements Coffee itself, holds a Coffee reference, and adds milk behavior while delegating everything else to the wrapped object.

The power is runtime composition. You can combine decorators in any order: new MilkDecorator(new SugarDecorator(new SimpleCoffee())). With inheritance you'd need a separate class for every combination. With decoration you compose freely.

non-obvious: Java IO uses this pattern throughout. BufferedReader wraps FileReader. GZIPInputStream wraps FileInputStream. Every wrapper is a decorator that adds behavior through composition. If Java had used inheritance instead, the class hierarchy would be enormous. Knowing this real-world example shows you've actually used composition in production code.

speakable_v2.cap: Decorator uses composition to combine behaviors at runtime. Much more flexible than a class per combination using inheritance.

question: How does the Decorator pattern use composition instead of inheritance?
title: Decorator pattern — composition to extend behavior at runtime
direct_answer: The Decorator pattern uses composition to add behavior to an object dynamically without subclassing. A decorator wraps the original object by holding it as a field that implements the same interface. The decorator implements the same interface, delegates to the wrapped object, and adds extra behavior before or after delegation. This allows combining features at runtime without the class explosion that would result from creating a subclass for every combination.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know a real design pattern that exemplifies composition over inheritance and can explain how it works with concrete details, not just memorized definitions.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Describing Decorator as a subclassing approach when it's specifically a composition-based pattern, or confusing it with inheritance-based patterns like Template Method.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect the Decorator pattern to a real Java example like BufferedReader wrapping FileReader, or mention how Spring's transaction proxies or caching annotations use decoration.

sections.title: Adding Behavior Through Wrapping Instead of Extending
sections.content:
The **Decorator pattern** is a textbook example of composition over inheritance — it lets you add new behavior to objects dynamically at runtime by wrapping them, rather than creating subclasses for every combination of features.

The key insight is that a decorator **implements the same interface** as the object it wraps and holds the wrapped object as a field. When a method is called on the decorator, it delegates to the wrapped object but adds extra behavior before or after the delegation.

Think of it like wrapping a gift — the gift box (decorator) contains the actual gift (component) and you can stack multiple boxes (decorators) on top of each other. This solves the **combinatorial explosion problem** that inheritance creates. If you want optional features like BufferedReading, Compression, and Encryption on a data stream, inheritance would require 2^3 = 8 subclasses for every combination. With decorators, you compose at runtime: new EncryptionDecorator(new CompressionDecorator(new BufferedReader(fileReader))). Each decorator adds one responsibility, and you stack them as needed. The Java I/O library (BufferedReader, LineNumberReader wrapping Reader) and Spring's transaction management both use this pattern.

sections.title: Decorator Pattern Composing Behavior at Runtime
When to Apply the Decorator Pattern
sections.content: **Use Decorator when** you need to add responsibilities to individual objects dynamically at runtime without affecting other objects of the same class. Classic scenarios: adding logging, caching, compression, encryption, or transaction management to services. In Spring Boot, this is exactly how the at-Transactional annotation works — Spring wraps your service bean in a transaction decorator proxy that starts a transaction before delegating to your method and commits after. **Decorator shines when** you have optional features that can be combined in different ways, and creating subclasses for every combination would be impractical. For example, a NotificationService might optionally add retry logic, rate limiting, and audit logging — with decorators, you compose these at runtime based on configuration. **Don't use Decorator when** the behavior change is fundamental to the object's identity (use inheritance or strategy pattern instead), or when you have only one enhancement and composition would be overkill.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Confusing Decorator with Inheritance**: Freshers think Decorator is about subclassing when it's specifically about composition — the decorator contains the wrapped object as a field, it doesn't extend it.
- **Breaking the Interface Contract**: Freshers create decorators that don't implement the same interface as the component, which breaks the pattern's core benefit of transparent substitution — you should be able to use a decorator anywhere the original component is expected.
- **Not Understanding Stacking**: Freshers think you can only have one decorator, missing that the pattern's power is stacking multiple decorators to compose behavior — each decorator wraps the previous one, creating a chain where each adds its behavior.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Composition Over Inheritance**: Decorator uses composition by holding the wrapped object as a field, not extending it as a subclass
**Same Interface**: Decorator implements the same interface as the component it wraps, enabling transparent substitution
**Delegation Plus Enhancement**: Decorator delegates to the wrapped object but adds behavior before or after delegation
**Avoids Class Explosion**: Combining N optional features with inheritance requires 2^N subclasses, decorators compose at runtime
**Stacking Decorators**: Multiple decorators can wrap each other, each adding one responsibility, creating a chain of behavior
**Real Java Examples**: BufferedReader wrapping FileReader, Spring transaction proxies, Java Servlet filters all use Decorator
**Runtime Composition**: Feature combinations are decided at runtime through object composition, not compile-time inheritance

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The Decorator pattern is a perfect example of composition over inheritance in action. Instead of creating subclasses to add behavior, you wrap an object with a decorator that implements the same interface. The decorator holds the original object as a field, and when its methods are called, it delegates to the wrapped object but adds extra behavior before or after. So if you have a DataSource interface with a readData method, you can create an EncryptionDecorator that wraps any DataSource, calls its readData method, and then encrypts the result before returning it. The key is that the decorator also implements DataSource, so you can use it anywhere the original is expected. The big win is you can stack decorators at runtime without creating tons of subclasses. If you want compression plus encryption, you wrap the original DataSource in a CompressionDecorator, then wrap that in an EncryptionDecorator. With inheritance, you'd need subclasses for every combination — PlainDataSource, EncryptedDataSource, CompressedDataSource, EncryptedAndCompressedDataSource — and it explodes as you add more features. A real-world Java example is BufferedReader wrapping FileReader in the I/O library. FileReader reads characters from a file, BufferedReader wraps it and adds buffering for efficiency. Both implement Reader, so you can use BufferedReader anywhere you'd use FileReader. In Spring, the at-Transactional annotation works through decoration — Spring wraps your service bean in a proxy that starts a transaction before calling your method and commits after. That's composition adding behavior at runtime, not inheritance. The pattern works best when you have optional features that need to combine in different ways and you want to avoid subclass explosion.
